title: A check must pass a known-good case
statement: Before trusting a check's rejections, run it over content known to be good, and treat its flags there as faults in the check.
example: A question set known to be good timed out on the same grading route, at 35.024 s and again at 90.020 s, while a single question scored 1.0 in 24.385 s.
detail: When locally valid new question sets kept timing out, a probe sent a known-good earlier set through the same scoring route as a control: it timed out too, at 35.024 s and again at 90.020 s under a longer cap, while single questions and short answers scored 1.0 SUPERIOR, which placed the block in the grader's route rather than in the content (notes of 23 and 24 May 2026). A guard for one war's name fired on the longer name of the next and failed three valid items, items about the later war were routed to the earlier war's template because its name matched, and two similarly named documents collided on one source key. A question-set validator's first version over-blocked known passing rows, and its hard gates were narrowed. A period check also flagged a founding document from inside the period asked about as later drift. Content known to be good includes known-good cases, near misses and items people approved. Narrow such a check, or demote it to information, when most of its hits land on sound content.
against: none found for the grading route and the name checks; for the period check, the reports never say what set the flag off, so whether it rejected a good document is open. The rule holds only while people read closely: the source says to revisit it if they stop, 'since the flag would then be the only judgment in the loop' (shadow-bench/docs/brainlift.md line 81). People can miss defects too, and 'nothing flows back from the classroom to reveal whether they missed any.' (line 143). These facts are the source's recollections, not records (line 181).
